stocks.transcript_raw: Investors, welcome to this morning's  financial interpretation. It is  currently Monday, October 19, 2026, at  8:31 AM Taipei time. Good morning,  everyone. Half an hour before the  market opens every day, we are here to  accompany you in interpreting  international financial news and  real-time changes. Things are very  exciting today, as tech stocks have  once again become the hardest-hit area  for selling pressure. Last week, the S& P 500 fell about 2%, while the Nasdaq  dropped 4.5%. It seems the more  tech-heavy, the steeper the decline,  especially for the SOX index, which  fell 11.4%in a single week, returning  directly to the correction lows of July  this year. So, this marks the largest  single-week decline since early April  2025. The last time we saw a drop of  over 10%in a week this severe was back  during the tariff wars. Especially this  time, regarding the selling pressure on  memory stocks, we saw Micron fall 14.6% for the week, and SK Hynix's ADR  dropped 16%. Although the VIX index has  risen, it seems to have just begun,  hovering around 19 to 21. It hasn't  reached extreme panic yet, so if it has  fallen this absurdly even before market  sentiment has fully fermented, could a  "Black Monday" be coming to the Taipei  stock market today? A master said I  would be troubled by "qing"(sentiments)  this year, so I couldn't help but sigh  at the sky—is it family, love, or  friendship? I never expected it to be " hangqing"(market trends)! We’ve been  live-streaming on this channel for  seven years now. You’ve accompanied  us through peaks, sleeping in parks,  meeting presidents, and visiting police  stations. What kind of storms haven't  we seen? Compared to the tariff wars,  this is actually manageable. The key is  to observe whether this market  situation is a crisis or an opportunity . Today, we will examine the pullback  in the US and global stock markets from  different angles to determine whether  the decline is concentrated in a single  index or if it is a broad, systematic  sell-off. The second point, of course,  is that we must clearly understand that  one thing can save the current state of  the US stock market, which is  coincidentally the cause of its decline : US Treasury yields. Having fallen  from 5.3%back to 5%, what is the only  good news now? With the stock market  falling like this to this point. If it  continues to drop like this every day,  the Fed simply has no grounds to raise  rates. Is it possible that because the  FOMC meeting is about to be held, the  stock market has adopted a certain  stance to force them not to raise rates ? We had originally anticipated it  fully, thinking, "Oh no, a rate hike is  coming in October." But with this kind  of collapse, how can they raise them?  This is a very interesting point to  observe; perhaps trading a moderate  valuation pullback for interest rate  stability is worth watching. Alright,  let’s look back; while global stock  markets are indeed pulling back, the  extent of this pullback varies  significantly. Looking at the Nasdaq  100 index, it is currently facing a  critical technical juncture. Based on  futures prices, the significant uptrend  line since April remains intact,  showing that there is still buying  interest at lower levels; it did break  below this key level last Friday, but  there is still some support from buyers  underneath. Even though AI financing  costs have risen, the core revenues of  these tech giants remain relatively  strong; we saw a first test between  July and August this year, followed by  a second test in September, and if it  can successfully hold this third wave,  it shows that market confidence remains  sufficient. The real disaster area  isn't actually the Nasdaq, but the  Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which  has fallen since its October 6th peak  by approximately......about 12%.  However, if we look from the absolute  high, the decline has nearly reached 20 %, technically entering a bear market;  but given the higher volatility of the  SOX index, a 20%drop isn't necessarily  alarming—it often gains 20%, so a 20% decline is quite normal. Look at the  beautiful gains from February, March,  and April this year; even if it has  entered a bear market now, it's still a  bull market from the beginning of the  year—it depends on your perspective,  but it has at least returned to the  lows seen around July. As for US  small-cap stocks, this wave has been  more painful, as the Russell 2000 index  has officially and completely fallen  below its yearly moving average. The  semiconductor sector really pushed the  overall valuation very high, so it is  at a certain distance from  medium-to-long-term moving averages,  allowing it to undergo a gradual  mid-term correction; this time, we see  that for small caps, especially in  five-year high-yield bonds, credit  spreads have widened to a six-month  high, and things like CDS prices and  their bond yields are all surging, so  since small caps rely more on external  financing to survive......when  borrowing costs rise rapidly and credit  spreads widen, the downward pressure on  stock prices is usually much greater.  Think about it carefully: if a large  tech stock in the Philadelphia  Semiconductor Index drops by 20%, it's  not the same as a US small-cap stock  dropping by 20%. The Philly Semi stocks  are at least still consistently  profitable with a solid core business.  As for the small-cap sector, many of  them actually rely on financing cycles  or borrowing costs just to keep staying  afloat. So overall, looking at the  market pullback between October 15th  and 16th, we now need to see if this  recent retreat in yields will give  small-cap stocks a chance to catch  their breath. Then look at the S&P 500;  it's actually doing fine, barely  dropping at all. You might even feel  that it's still oscillating at a high  level. One can only say that market  panic is slowly rising. The S&P is  currently around 7,700 points, having  pulled back near the 100-day moving  average. It's still in a sideways  consolidation range from the past few  months, quite a distance from the  yearly moving average, which means the  overall impact on the major indices  isn't as big as imagined. The panic  seems to be specifically targeting  small-cap stocks on one hand, and  hardware-related Philly Semi stocks  that saw exceptionally high gains from  February to March of this year on the  other. Next, let's look at the South  Korean stock market. The EWY ETF is now  about ready to test its yearly moving  average. Because the KOSPI index had  such impressive gains this year, even  with a 20%drop, it still remains among  the top performers globally in terms of  year-to-date gains. If you look at the  South Korean KOSPI index from its early  October high of 6,970 points, it has  now fallen to around 5,550. A 20%drop  in one week is truly outrageous—it's  incredible that the broader market  could fall 20%in just a week. It is  worth noting that this wave of selling  is also related to domestic buying in  South Korea. Their situation is similar  to Taiwan's, where foreign capital is  constantly selling, offloading hundreds  of billions at a time. The key point is  that investors in the Taipei stock  market are very wealthy; they are  willing to buy whatever foreign capital  sells. That's why you always feel like  the market bounces back after opening  low—they can't help but enter the  market. The Korean market used to be  like this, so why is the buying power  so weak this time? The reason lies in  the fact that the Korean market  previously saw high-intensity share  buybacks from major firms like Samsung  and SK Hynix, but last week, that  buyback volume was cut in half. Looking  at the cumulative scale, it has reached  about 55 trillion NTD. Now that the  buyback plans are coming to an end, the  funds that originally supported stock  prices have suddenly dried up. This  means the capital from corporate  insiders and major shareholders didn't  step in last week, and prices collapsed . This is a key point to observe,  implying that the Taiwan stock market  has actually been relying on domestic  funds. If anyone wavers, prices could  see a significant correction. Regarding  Taiwan stocks, when will the  institutional investors actually take  action? I feel that market volatility  is quite high right now, but you  haven't really seen retail investors in  the Taipei stock market ever truly lose  confidence over the past few years. Because memory  stocks are inherently a hard-hit area,  their selling pressure is even heavier  than the pressure on Taiwan's advanced  manufacturing processes, specifically  TSMC. Looking at the past period,  Samsung and SK Hynix fell by about 20% and 26%respectively in one week.  Foreign investors have been net sellers  of Korean tech stocks for eight  consecutive trading days, totaling  about 11.6 billion USD. Hedging funds  are also exiting positions with high  intensity. The market is especially  worried about another factor: YMTC's  global DRAM revenue market share has  reached about 10%. After this  correction, the market worries that  even if market supply capacity only  gradually opens up by 2028 or 2029,  there is still fear that valuations  have been priced in too early. But I  don't think it's that bad, because  Samsung's price-to-book ratio is  currently only 1.2 x, and SK Hynix's is  only 0.9 x, so you can't say their  valuations are ridiculously high.  However, the gains from the long rally  seem to have become a reason for a  market pullback. During this correction , it also hints that as long as bond  yields drop enough, perhaps the selling  pressure won't be as intense, since the  previous pressure stemmed from high  yields. Looking at the weekly charts  for memory and storage equipment stocks —like SanDisk, Western Digital, and  Micron—they all experienced  high-level pullbacks after a long  period of surging. In the short term,  you might feel like the market is  crashing, with drops of 20%common, but  if you look from February until now,  doesn't it just feel like a breather?  So, this is looking at things from  different scales. As viewers comment in  the chat, what is our famous saying?  Don't mistake the fluctuations for the  trend. Of course, the chances of being  right or wrong about the trend are high , but in the long run, we believe the  trend is heading toward that 45-degree  angle in the upper right. However,  don't focus on the fluctuations; don't  get shaken out every time there's a  correction. Clearly, from the beginning  of this year until now, it's still been  a bull market, so why are so many  people losing money? Now, regarding the Taipei stock market,  many say AI stocks are facing  correction pressure, but I think it's  more about whether the Taipei market is  experiencing significant buying  momentum. If you compare the Taiwan  stock market with the Korean market,  you'll find that when Taiwan stocks  rise, they move with Korea, but when  the Korean market falls, Taiwan stocks  don't budge. This shows that domestic  buying in Taiwan is actually stronger  than imagined. Could it be that the  Korean stock market is just that  unappealing? Because that market is too  tech-heavy and consists of cyclical  stocks, foreign investors sell heavily.  That's one perspective, but looking at  the forex market, the sell-off pressure  from foreign investors is actually very , very heavy for both. We saw that at  one point, the South Korean market  plummeted by 8%intraday, while the  Taipei market fell by 3%. Foreign  investors sold a record 93 billion in  Taiwan stocks at the time, so both the  Korean Won and the New Taiwan Dollar  were depreciating in sync. The point is  that, looking at domestic buying, it's  mainly because major shareholders in  the Korean market, or what we call  stock buybacks, have weakened slightly.  Later on, because the U.S. stock market  took a heavy hit on Friday, the Taipei  stock market will likely see volatility  at Monday's opening. But investors, the  market can't rise forever without  falling; if you don't crouch down, how  can you jump higher next time? If you  don't hold during a downturn, you won't  have anything to sell during an upturn.  The market won't stop falling just  because we're afraid. It won't stop  because of our fear, and it won't wait  for us to get on board just because  we're hesitant. What truly determines  long-term returns isn't how much you  made when the market was good, but  whether you can maintain your  discipline, hold your positions, and  even seize opportunities when others  panic during bad times.
